option_description: Controls whether full-disk or volume-level encryption (e.g., BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS, LUKS on Linux) is active on the device, ensuring all stored data is cryptographically protected at rest.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'disk_encryption_disabled_or_partial' exposure whenever this attribute is false or absent. Without encryption, a physically seized or stolen device exposes all stored credentials, organizational data, and cached secrets in cleartext. This is classified as high criticality (score 8) because physical access alone is sufficient to extract data without bypassing OS authentication.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, check BitLocker status for all volumes using the built-in manage-bde tool.
how_to_obtain.command: manage-bde -status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each volume should report 'Protection Status: Protection On' and 'Conversion Status: Fully Encrypted'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, query FileVault status using fdesetup.
how_to_obtain.command: fdesetup status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should read 'FileVault is On.' for encryption to be considered active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, check LUKS encryption status for the root or data block device using cryptsetup.
how_to_obtain.command: cryptsetup status /dev/mapper/$(lsblk -o NAME,TYPE | awk '/crypt/{print $1}' | head -1)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show 'type: LUKS2' and 'cipher:' fields, confirming an active encrypted mapping.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM/UEM compliance API (e.g., Microsoft Intune Graph API) to retrieve encryption compliance state for a specific device.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>?$select=isEncrypted,deviceName'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response should contain '"isEncrypted": true' for the device to be considered compliant.

option_description: Describes how broadly disk encryption is applied across the device: 'full' means every volume and partition is encrypted, 'partial' means only selected partitions (e.g., only the OS drive, leaving secondary data drives unencrypted), and 'none' means no encryption is applied anywhere.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'disk_encryption_disabled_or_partial' not only when encryption is fully absent but also explicitly when encryption_scope is 'partial' even if full_disk_encryption_enabled is true. This prevents a false sense of security where an OS volume is encrypted but a secondary data drive holding organizational files, cached credentials, or downloaded documents remains readable after physical seizure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, enumerate all volumes and their BitLocker protection status to identify any unencrypted volumes.
how_to_obtain.command: manage-bde -status | Select-String -Pattern 'Volume|Protection Status|Conversion Status'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Every listed volume should show 'Protection Status: Protection On'. Any volume showing 'Protection Off' indicates partial scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, list all APFS volumes and check whether FileVault encryption extends to non-system volumes using diskutil.
how_to_obtain.command: diskutil apfs list | grep -E 'Volume|Encryption'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All data volumes should report 'Encryption: Yes' or inherit FileVault from the container; any 'Encryption: No' indicates partial scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, list all block devices and identify which are backed by a LUKS crypt device versus exposed as plaintext partitions.
how_to_obtain.command: lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT | grep -v 'loop'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Partitions with sensitive mount points (/, /home, /data) should show TYPE 'crypt' or be children of a crypt device. Plaintext partitions at sensitive mount points indicate partial scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, navigate to Devices > Monitor > Encryption report to view per-device encryption coverage across all enrolled devices.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Devices > Monitor > Encryption report
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Devices with full encryption show status 'Encrypted'; devices showing 'Not encrypted' or with partial coverage are flagged.

option_description: Controls whether the device enforces an automatic lock screen requiring authentication (PIN, password, pattern, or biometric) when the device is idle or after a defined timeout period, preventing unauthorized access to an unattended device.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'weak_or_absent_screen_lock_authentication' (high criticality, score 8) immediately when screen_lock_enabled is false or absent. Without a screen lock, any person with physical access to an unattended device gains immediate access to all applications, credentials, organizational email, and data. This is a prerequisite control that all subsequent screen lock strength checks depend on — if this is false, no further lock assessment is meaningful.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Intune device compliance details via Microsoft Graph API to check whether the device satisfies the screen lock compliance policy.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>?$select=complianceState,deviceName,osVersion'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A compliant device with an active screen lock policy enforced will return 'complianceState: compliant'. Cross-reference with the assigned compliance policy to confirm screen lock is a requirement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android devices (via ADB), query the secure settings to confirm a screen lock type is configured.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell settings get secure lockscreen.password_type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A value of 0 indicates no lock screen. Values 65536 (pattern), 131072 (PIN), or 262144 (password) indicate an active screen lock.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, check whether a screen saver password (lock-on-resume) is enforced via registry policy.
how_to_obtain.command: reg query 'HKCU\Control Panel\Desktop' /v ScreenSaverIsSecure
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A value of '0x1' confirms the screen saver requires a password on resume, effectively enforcing a screen lock. A value of '0x0' or missing key indicates no enforced lock.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS, inspect the MDM configuration profile assigned to the device to confirm a passcode policy is included.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Apple Configurator or MDM Console > Devices > [Select Device] > Profiles > Passcode Policy
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A Passcode Policy profile present in the device profile list confirms screen lock is MDM-enforced. Absence of this profile indicates the device may have no enforced lock.

option_description: Specifies the authentication mechanism used to unlock the device screen, ranging from no lock or swipe (no security), through pattern or PIN, to password or biometric authentication. This determines the effective strength of physical access control on the device.
security_impact: The Rego policy evaluates screen_lock_type in multiple conditions within 'weak_or_absent_screen_lock_authentication'. Values of 'none' or 'swipe' trigger the exposure regardless of other settings, as they provide no real authentication barrier. 'biometric_only' triggers the exposure when the fallback factor is weak, because biometrics can be bypassed (e.g., spoofing, forced unlock) and the fallback becomes the actual security boundary. 'pin' and 'password' types are further evaluated against minimum passcode length.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android devices via ADB, retrieve the numeric lock type code from secure settings.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell settings get secure lockscreen.password_type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Mapping: 0=none, 1=swipe, 65536=pattern, 131072=PIN, 262144=password. Values 327680 or 393216 indicate biometric-based locks depending on manufacturer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve iOS/iPadOS passcode compliance settings from an MDM console (e.g., Jamf Pro) using the device management API.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u 'admin:password' -H 'Accept: application/json' 'https://<jamf-server>/JSSResource/mobiledevices/id/<deviceId>'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The response JSON should include a 'PasscodePresent' boolean and 'PasscodeCompliant' field. Check the assigned MDM profile for the allowed passcode types (numeric, alphanumeric, biometric).

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, review the device compliance policy assigned to the device to see what lock types are permitted or required.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Devices > Compliance Policies > [Policy Name] > Properties > System Security > Required password type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The policy should specify a minimum required type such as 'Alphanumeric' or 'Numeric with no repeating or ordered sequences'. A setting of 'Device default' or 'Low security biometric' indicates weak enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, check the Group Policy or Intune policy-applied setting for password complexity requirement enforced on the lock screen.
how_to_obtain.command: secedit /export /cfg C:\secpolicy.cfg && findstr /i 'PasswordComplexity MinimumPasswordLength' C:\secpolicy.cfg
how_to_obtain.expected_output: PasswordComplexity=1 and MinimumPasswordLength>=8 indicate a strong password-type lock is enforced. PasswordComplexity=0 indicates simple or no complexity requirement.

option_description: Defines the minimum number of characters or digits required for the device screen lock passcode or PIN as enforced by MDM policy. This sets a floor on brute-force resistance for the lock screen credential.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'weak_or_absent_screen_lock_authentication' when screen_lock_type is 'pin', 'password', or 'pattern_simple' and minimum_passcode_length is less than 4. A 4-digit PIN has only 10,000 combinations and is considered a bare minimum threshold; policies should target 6+ digits for PINs and 8+ characters for passwords. Short PINs are trivially brute-forced offline if the encrypted device storage is extracted without the hardware throttling that makes online brute-force slower.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Android EMM (Enterprise Mobility Management) API or Google Workspace MDM policy to retrieve the enforced minimum password length setting.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://androidmanagement.googleapis.com/v1/enterprises/<enterpriseId>/policies/<policyId>' | python3 -c "import sys,json; p=json.load(sys.stdin); print(p.get('passwordPolicies', 'Not set'))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The 'passwordPolicies' object should include a 'passwordMinimumLength' field. A value below 6 for PIN or below 8 for password type should be flagged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For iOS/iPadOS devices managed by Jamf Pro, retrieve the minimum passcode length from the configuration profile XML.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u 'admin:password' -H 'Accept: application/xml' 'https://<jamf-server>/JSSResource/mobiledeviceConfigurationProfiles/id/<profileId>' | xmllint --xpath '//minPasscodeLength/text()' -
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The command should return an integer. A value of 0 or absence of the element indicates no minimum length is enforced by the profile.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, inspect the iOS or Android compliance policy to view the enforced minimum password length.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Devices > Compliance Policies > [Policy Name] > Properties > System Security > Minimum password length
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The field should show a value of 6 or higher for PINs and 8 or higher for alphanumeric passwords. A value of 0 or 'Not configured' means no minimum is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, export and inspect the local or domain security policy for the minimum password length requirement.
how_to_obtain.command: net accounts | findstr /i 'Minimum password length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output such as 'Minimum password length: 8' indicates an enforced minimum. A value of 0 means no minimum is set and must be remediated via Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Password Policy > Minimum password length).

option_description: Specifies the fallback authentication method that becomes active when biometric authentication fails, is exhausted after repeated attempts, or is deliberately bypassed. This is the actual security boundary when biometrics are circumvented, as the fallback credential is what an attacker must defeat if biometric spoofing is not viable.
security_impact: The Rego policy explicitly triggers 'weak_or_absent_screen_lock_authentication' when screen_lock_type is 'biometric_only' or 'biometric_with_fallback' and biometric_fallback_factor is 'none', 'swipe', or 'weak_pin'. This reflects a critical security reality: biometric systems on mobile devices are designed to fall back to a PIN/password, and if that fallback is weak, the entire lock screen security collapses. Attackers can intentionally trigger biometric failures (e.g., multiple failed fingerprint attempts) to force the weaker fallback and exploit it via brute force or shoulder surfing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM policy for iOS/Android to determine what fallback is configured alongside biometric authentication in the passcode policy profile.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u 'admin:password' -H 'Accept: application/json' 'https://<jamf-server>/JSSResource/mobiledeviceConfigurationProfiles/id/<profileId>' | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A5 'passcodePol'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The passcode policy should show allowSimple=false, minLength>=6, and requireAlphanumeric=true if a strong password fallback is required. Simple numeric-only settings of length 4 or less indicate weak_pin fallback.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Android via ADB, query the password quality setting which reflects the effective fallback requirement when biometric fails.
how_to_obtain.command: adb shell dpm get-password-quality
how_to_obtain.expected_output: PASSWORD_QUALITY_ALPHANUMERIC or PASSWORD_QUALITY_COMPLEX indicates a strong fallback. PASSWORD_QUALITY_NUMERIC_COMPLEX (minimum) maps to strong_pin. PASSWORD_QUALITY_SOMETHING or PASSWORD_QUALITY_NUMERIC maps to weak_pin or swipe.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, inspect the Android or iOS compliance policy to confirm the fallback password type and minimum length are configured beyond basic PIN.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Devices > Compliance Policies > [Policy Name] > System Security > Required password type and Minimum password length
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The required password type should be set to 'Alphanumeric' or 'Numeric with no repeating or ordered sequences' with a minimum length of at least 6. A type of 'At least numeric' with length 4 or less indicates a weak_pin fallback configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organizational MDM policy documentation or enrollment profile specifications to confirm the biometric fallback strength requirement is explicitly defined and enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy documentation should explicitly state that biometric authentication must be backed by a strong PIN (minimum 6 digits, no repeating sequences) or alphanumeric password. Absence of this requirement or a stated minimum below 6 digits indicates a policy gap.

option_description: Controls whether standard (non-IT) end users are members of the local Administrators group on their workstations. When true, the user has persistent elevated privileges over the entire operating system, including the ability to install software, modify security settings, and bypass standard user restrictions.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'local_administrator_privileges_granted_to_standard_users' exposure when this attribute is true AND privileged_access_management_enforced is false. Persistent local admin rights allow malware to install without UAC prompts, attackers to disable security tools, and users to circumvent application controls — all without additional authentication. Eliminating persistent admin rights is a primary defense against lateral movement and privilege escalation chains.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, query the local Administrators group membership directly from an elevated command prompt or via remote PowerShell to list all members.
how_to_obtain.command:
net localgroup Administrators
# OR via PowerShell for remote bulk query:
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' | Select-Object Name, PrincipalSource
# For domain-wide inventory via PowerShell remoting:
Invoke-Command -ComputerName (Get-ADComputer -Filter *).Name -ScriptBlock { Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' }
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output lists group members; non-IT user accounts (e.g., DOMAIN\jsmith) present in this list indicate standard_users_have_local_admin = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, use dscl to read the admin group membership and identify non-IT user accounts.
how_to_obtain.command:
dscl . -read /Groups/admin GroupMembership
# Also check via:
dscacheutil -q group -a name admin
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns a space-separated list of usernames; any standard end-user account listed confirms local admin membership.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune or a comparable MDM console, navigate to device compliance reports or endpoint analytics to review local administrator membership policy compliance across the fleet.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Intune Admin Center → Devices → All Devices → [Select Device] → Device configuration profiles → Account Protection profile → Review local admin settings; or Reports → Endpoint Analytics → Device compliance
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Compliance report flags devices where standard users are in the local Administrators group, or where a local admin restriction policy is not applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Microsoft Graph API to retrieve device compliance status or configuration profile assignment results for local administrator controls.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -X GET 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices?$select=deviceName,complianceState,userPrincipalName' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response listing managed devices with compliance state; cross-reference with GPO/Account Protection profile targeting local admin restrictions.

typical_values: true (common in SMBs and legacy environments without MDM enforcement)
false (target state enforced via GPO, MDM, or PAM tooling)

option_description: Indicates whether a Privileged Access Management solution — such as CyberArk Endpoint Privilege Manager, BeyondTrust EPM, or Ivanti Application Control — is deployed and actively enforcing just-in-time elevation or application allow-listing with elevation. This replaces persistent local administrator rights with on-demand, audited privilege grants.
security_impact: The Rego policy only fires the 'local_administrator_privileges_granted_to_standard_users' exposure when standard_users_have_local_admin is true AND this attribute is false. A deployed PAM solution is the accepted compensating control: even if a user technically needs admin-level operations, those are mediated through policy-controlled elevation with logging, preventing uncontrolled persistent access. Without PAM enforcement, persistent admin rights remain a direct attack surface for malware, insider threats, and privilege escalation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the PAM vendor management console (e.g., CyberArk EPM Console, BeyondTrust EPM Management Console) for agent deployment coverage and active policy enforcement status.
how_to_obtain.navigation: CyberArk EPM Console → Computers → All Computers → Filter by 'Agent Status' = Active; or BeyondTrust EPM → Computers → Deployment Status → Confirm 'Managed' state and active policy applied
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All enrolled workstations show agent status as 'Active' and a privilege management policy assigned and enforced; gaps indicate privileged_access_management_enforced = false for those devices.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows endpoints, verify that the PAM agent service is installed and running, and confirm an active policy is applied.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Check for CyberArk EPM agent:
Get-Service -Name 'CyberArk Endpoint Privilege Manager Agent' | Select-Object Status
# Check for BeyondTrust EPM:
Get-Service -Name 'Defendpoint' | Select-Object Status
# Verify Ivanti Application Control:
Get-Service -Name 'AppSense Application Manager' | Select-Object Status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service status returns 'Running'; absence or 'Stopped' state confirms PAM is not enforced on that device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM or endpoint management API to retrieve compliance policy results for PAM agent deployment.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Example for Microsoft Intune Graph API — retrieve device configuration profile assignment:
curl -X GET 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/deviceConfigurationDeviceStatuses' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
# Filter for the PAM agent deployment profile to confirm 'succeeded' state per device
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Devices with 'succeeded' status for the PAM deployment configuration profile confirm enforcement; 'failed' or 'not applicable' devices are non-compliant.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the endpoint security or IT operations team to confirm whether a PAM product is licensed, deployed, and has active policies covering all workstation tiers, including privileged and BYOD devices.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation of PAM product name, version, deployment percentage across fleet, and active policy names; absence of documentation or partial deployment confirms the attribute may be false.

typical_values: false (majority of organizations without mature endpoint privilege programs)
true (organizations with CyberArk EPM, BeyondTrust EPM, or Ivanti Application Control fully deployed)

option_description: Captures the operational state of the antivirus, Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), or host-based intrusion prevention system installed on the workstation. Valid states are 'active' (fully operational), 'disabled' (installed but turned off), 'tampered' (integrity of the agent has been compromised or its processes killed), and 'not_installed' (no protection agent present).
security_impact: The Rego policy directly triggers the 'endpoint_protection_disabled_or_tampered' exposure for any status value of 'not_installed', 'disabled', or 'tampered'. Even when 'active', additional conditions on signature age and broad exclusions can still fire the exposure. A non-active status completely removes detection and prevention capability from the device, leaving it blind to malware execution, credential harvesting, and lateral movement activities that EDR telemetry would otherwise surface.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the endpoint security management console (e.g., Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne) for agent health status per device.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Defender Portal (security.microsoft.com) → Endpoints → Devices → Filter by 'Sensor health state' = Inactive or Misconfigured; CrowdStrike Falcon → Hosts → Host Management → Filter by 'Status' ≠ Normal
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Devices not showing 'Active/Healthy' sensor status correspond to endpoint_protection_status values of 'disabled', 'tampered', or 'not_installed'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, query the Windows Security Center WMI namespace and the Defender service status to determine active protection state.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Check Windows Defender / Security Center status:
Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AMRunningMode, AMServiceEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, TamperProtectionSource
# Check third-party AV registration:
Get-CimInstance -Namespace root/SecurityCenter2 -ClassName AntivirusProduct | Select-Object displayName, productState
# Check EDR service (CrowdStrike example):
Get-Service -Name 'CSFalconService' | Select-Object Status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RealTimeProtectionEnabled = True and AMServiceEnabled = True indicates 'active'; False values or missing EDR service indicate 'disabled' or 'not_installed'; tampered state is indicated by productState hex code anomalies or service in a failed state with evidence of forceful termination.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the EDR vendor API or Microsoft Graph Security API for device sensor health telemetry across the fleet.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Microsoft Defender for Endpoint via Graph:
curl -X GET 'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/machines?$filter=healthStatus ne 'Active'' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
# CrowdStrike Falcon API:
curl -X GET 'https://api.crowdstrike.com/devices/queries/devices/v1?filter=status:!"normal"' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns a list of devices where sensor health is not 'Active'; these devices map to endpoint_protection_status values other than 'active'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM alerts or endpoint security event logs for tamper protection events, service termination events (Event ID 7045, 7034, 7036), or absence of expected EDR telemetry heartbeats.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-WinEvent -LogName System | Where-Object {$_.Id -in @(7034, 7036, 7045) -and $_.Message -like '*Falcon*' -or $_.Message -like '*Defender*'} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Events showing EDR/AV service crash, stop, or unexpected termination indicate 'tampered' or 'disabled' status; absence of expected heartbeat events in SIEM confirms potential 'not_installed' state.

typical_values: active (well-managed corporate fleets with MDM enforcement)
disabled (devices with user-disabled protection or policy gaps)
tampered (targeted attacks or advanced malware attempting to blind EDR)
not_installed (unmanaged or newly provisioned devices, BYOD without MAM)

option_description: Records the number of days elapsed since the endpoint protection software last successfully downloaded and applied an updated threat signature or definition database. A high value indicates the device's AV/EDR detections are operating against an outdated threat landscape, missing newly discovered malware families and IOCs.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'endpoint_protection_disabled_or_tampered' exposure when endpoint_protection_status is 'active' but signature_age_days exceeds 7 days. Signatures older than one week miss hundreds of new malware variants released daily. Ransomware families, infostealers, and commodity trojans often evade older signatures by design, specifically targeting organizations with delayed update cadences. An active EDR with stale definitions provides false confidence while leaving detection gaps.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, query Windows Defender's last signature update time and compute the delta in days using PowerShell.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Get Defender signature age:
$status = Get-MpComputerStatus
$lastUpdate = $status.AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated
$ageDays = (Get-Date) - $lastUpdate
Write-Output "Signature age: $($ageDays.Days) days (Last updated: $lastUpdate)"

# For third-party AV, check product-specific WMI or registry:
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Symantec\Symantec Endpoint Protection\AV\PatternManager' | Select-Object 'LatestDefsDate'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns the last update timestamp; compute days delta against current date. Values > 7 indicate the threshold is breached per policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the AV/EDR management console for per-device definition update timestamps, filtering for devices with outdated signatures beyond the acceptable threshold.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Defender Portal → Reports → Endpoint protection report → Antivirus status → Filter 'Antivirus signature age' > 7 days; CrowdStrike Falcon → Hosts → Host Management → Add filter 'Last Seen' to identify stale agents; SentinelOne → Endpoints → Filter by 'Threat Intelligence Date'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Dashboard displays a list of devices with signature ages exceeding policy threshold; these devices have signature_age_days values triggering the Rego exposure rule.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint REST API to retrieve antivirus definition version and update dates per machine.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -X GET 'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/machines' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' | jq '.value[] | {computerDnsName, avSignatureVersion, avSignatureUpdateTime}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output showing avSignatureUpdateTime per device; calculate days since that timestamp to derive signature_age_days per machine.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query SIEM for AV signature update success/failure events forwarded from endpoints, looking for devices with no successful update event in the past 7 days.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Example Splunk SPL query:
index=endpoint sourcetype=WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational EventCode=2000
| eval signature_update_time=strptime(_time, "%Y-%m-%d")
| stats latest(signature_update_time) as last_update by host
| eval age_days=round((now()-last_update)/86400,0)
| where age_days > 7
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of hostnames where the last successful signature update event is older than 7 days, indicating elevated signature_age_days values.

typical_values: 0-1 (well-managed fleet with automatic updates and internet connectivity)
2-7 (acceptable range, typical for devices with intermittent connectivity)
8-30 (policy-violating; common on VPN-disconnected or offline devices)
30+ (severely outdated; common on BYOD or unmanaged machines, air-gapped devices)

option_description: Contains the list of filesystem paths or glob patterns configured as scan exclusions within the endpoint protection tool. Exclusions prevent the AV/EDR from inspecting files, processes, or directories matching these patterns. 'Broad' exclusions are those covering large attack surfaces such as root drives, system directories (%TEMP%, %APPDATA%, C:\Windows\System32), entire user profile trees, or application installation directories.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'endpoint_protection_disabled_or_tampered' exposure when endpoint_protection_status is 'active' but count(broad_exclusion_paths) > 0. Overly broad exclusions are a well-documented attacker technique: after gaining initial access, threat actors modify AV exclusion lists to stage malware in excluded directories where it will never be scanned. Even pre-existing broad exclusions set by IT (often to reduce false positives) create permanent blind spots that malware authors specifically target, placing payloads in %TEMP% or %APPDATA% precisely because these are commonly excluded.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, enumerate all configured Windows Defender exclusion paths, extensions, and processes using PowerShell to identify overly broad entries.
how_to_obtain.command:
# List all Defender exclusions:
Get-MpPreference | Select-Object ExclusionPath, ExclusionExtension, ExclusionProcess, ExclusionIpAddress | Format-List

# Flag high-risk exclusions with a filter:
$exclusions = (Get-MpPreference).ExclusionPath
$broadPatterns = @('C:\\', 'C:\\Windows', 'C:\\Users', '%TEMP%', '%APPDATA%', '*', 'C:\\Windows\\System32')
$exclusions | Where-Object { $_ -in $broadPatterns -or $_ -match '\*' }
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lists all exclusion paths; entries matching root drives, system directories, or wildcard patterns populate the broad_exclusion_paths array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Export or review the exclusion list from the AV/EDR management console, filtering for entries that cover broad or high-risk directories.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Defender Portal → Configuration Management → Endpoint Security Policies → Antivirus → Review 'Exclusions' configuration; CrowdStrike Falcon → Configure → Prevention Policies → Exclusions → Export list; Symantec/SEP Manager → Policies → Virus and Spyware Protection → Exceptions → Export
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exported exclusion list; analyst reviews for entries covering root volumes (C:\), system paths (System32, Temp, AppData), or wildcard patterns (*.*, C:\Users\*).

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS with third-party EDR agents, review the agent's local configuration file for exclusion definitions.
how_to_obtain.command:
# CrowdStrike Falcon on macOS:
cat /Library/CS/falconctl
# Check exclusion configurations for SentinelOne:
sentinelctl status
# Symantec Endpoint Protection:
cat '/Library/Application Support/Symantec/Symantec Endpoint Protection/exclusions.xml'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration file contents reveal exclusion paths; entries covering /tmp, /var/folders, /Users, or / are considered broad and should be flagged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the EDR platform API to retrieve the current exclusion list programmatically for bulk assessment across devices.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Microsoft Defender for Endpoint - retrieve indicators/exclusions:
curl -X GET 'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/indicators?$filter=indicatorType eq 'FilePath'' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' | jq '.value[] | {indicatorValue, action}'

# CrowdStrike Falcon - retrieve exclusions:
curl -X GET 'https://api.crowdstrike.com/exclusions/queries/ml-exclusions/v1' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON list of configured exclusion paths; filter for entries matching broad path patterns to populate broad_exclusion_paths.

typical_values: ['C:\\', 'C:\\Windows\\Temp', '%APPDATA%', 'C:\\Windows\\System32'] (severely misconfigured; often set to suppress false positives without risk assessment)
['C:\\ProgramData', 'C:\\Windows\\SoftwareDistribution'] (moderate risk; common in poorly scoped vendor-recommended exclusions)

option_description: Measures the number of days that have elapsed since the vendor released a critical patch (OS, driver, or UEFI/BIOS firmware) that the workstation has not yet applied. This is a real-time lag indicator: a value of 0 means the device is fully current on critical patches, while higher values indicate increasingly stale patch state and growing window of exploitability for known vulnerabilities.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses this attribute in the 'os_and_firmware_patching_lag' exposure rule, firing when days_since_critical_patch_available > 0 combined with a non-empty patch_scope. Critical patches address publicly disclosed CVEs — often with available public exploits — in OS components, kernel drivers, and firmware. Every day beyond the patch release date extends the window during which attackers can exploit known vulnerabilities using commodity exploit kits, wormable exploits (e.g., EternalBlue-class), or targeted attacks referencing public CVE PoC code.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the patch management or MDM console to compare each device's installed patch level against the latest critical patch release date from the vendor.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Intune → Reports → Windows Updates → Windows Feature and Quality Update Reports → Review 'Deployment status' and 'Days since update available'; WSUS → Update Services → Computers → [Select computer] → Needed Updates → Filter by 'Classification: Critical Updates'; Ivanti Patch Management → Scan Results → Filter by 'Severity: Critical' and 'Status: Missing'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Report shows per-device count of days since each critical patch was available but not applied; maximum value across all missing critical patches is the days_since_critical_patch_available value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, query Windows Update history and the list of missing updates using PowerShell to calculate the oldest uninstalled critical patch date.
how_to_obtain.command:
# List missing critical updates and their release dates:
$UpdateSession = New-Object -ComObject Microsoft.Update.Session
$UpdateSearcher = $UpdateSession.CreateUpdateSearcher()
$SearchResult = $UpdateSearcher.Search("IsInstalled=0 and Type='Software' and IsHidden=0")
$SearchResult.Updates | Where-Object {$_.MsrcSeverity -eq 'Critical'} | Select-Object Title, LastDeploymentChangeTime | Sort-Object LastDeploymentChangeTime

# Calculate days since oldest critical patch:
$oldest = ($SearchResult.Updates | Where-Object {$_.MsrcSeverity -eq 'Critical'} | Sort-Object LastDeploymentChangeTime | Select-Object -First 1).LastDeploymentChangeTime
$daysDelta = (Get-Date) - $oldest
Write-Output "Days since oldest critical patch available: $($daysDelta.Days)"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows the release date of the oldest uninstalled critical patch and computes the lag in days; this is the days_since_critical_patch_available value for the device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Microsoft Graph API for Windows Update compliance reports or use the Defender for Endpoint vulnerability management API to retrieve missing patch data.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Defender for Endpoint - get software vulnerabilities and associated patch dates:
curl -X GET 'https://api.securitycenter.microsoft.com/api/machines/<machineId>/vulnerabilities?$filter=cvssV3 ge 7.0' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' | jq '.value[] | {cveId, publishedOn, patchPublishedOn}'

# Compute days since patchPublishedOn for each unpatched critical CVE
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON list of vulnerabilities per machine with patch publication dates; compute the maximum days delta between patchPublishedOn and current date across all critical unpatched vulnerabilities.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review patch management system logs or SIEM data for patch installation success/failure events to identify devices with the longest gap since a critical patch was applied.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Splunk SPL to identify devices with critical patches not applied within threshold:
index=patch_management severity=critical status=missing
| eval days_lag=round((now()-strptime(patch_release_date,"%Y-%m-%d"))/86400,0)
| stats max(days_lag) as max_days_since_patch by hostname
| where max_days_since_patch > 0
| sort -max_days_since_patch
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ranked list of devices with the number of days since the most recent uninstalled critical patch was released; highest values indicate worst patch lag.

typical_values: 0 (fully patched; achievable with auto-update enabled and healthy MDM connectivity)
1-14 (acceptable lag for patch testing and ring deployment cycles)
15-30 (approaching policy violation threshold; common in environments with manual patch approval workflows)
30-90 (policy-violating; frequently observed on BYOD, remote devices with poor MDM connectivity, or organizations with lengthy change management gates)
90+ (critical risk; common on legacy systems, air-gapped devices, or where patching is systematically deferred)

option_description: Identifies which categories of critical patches remain unapplied on the device. Valid elements are 'os' (operating system updates), 'driver' (hardware driver updates), and 'uefi_bios' (firmware updates). An empty array indicates no outstanding critical patches.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Os And Firmware Patching Lag' exposure whenever patch_scope is non-empty and days_since_critical_patch_available is greater than zero. A non-empty patch_scope means known, exploitable vulnerabilities remain unpatched. The policy also applies a dedicated condition when 'uefi_bios' is present in the scope, reflecting the elevated risk of firmware-level vulnerabilities that persist across OS reinstalls and are not addressed by standard OS patch management.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, navigate to Devices > All Devices, select the target device, then review 'Device compliance' and 'Windows Update rings' status. Cross-reference against the 'Update status' blade to identify pending OS, driver, and firmware updates.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Intune portal > Devices > All Devices > [Device] > Update status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of pending updates categorized by type (Quality, Driver, BIOS/Firmware). Any critical-severity pending item maps to an element in patch_scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, use PowerShell to query the Windows Update Agent for pending updates and classify them by category (OS, driver, UEFI/BIOS).
how_to_obtain.command: Get-WindowsUpdate -Category 'Critical Updates','Driver','BIOS' -NotInstalled | Select-Object Title, KB, Categories | Format-List
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of unapplied updates. Entries containing 'Driver' in Categories map to 'driver'; entries containing 'BIOS' or 'Firmware' map to 'uefi_bios'; remaining OS entries map to 'os'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, use the package manager to list available security updates. For UEFI firmware, query fwupd for pending firmware updates.
how_to_obtain.command: apt-get -s upgrade 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'security' ; fwupdmgr get-updates 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'Name|Version|Urgency'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Security package lines indicate 'os' scope. fwupdmgr output listing available UEFI or driver firmware updates indicates 'uefi_bios' or 'driver' scope respectively.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Microsoft Graph API to query a device's Windows Update compliance state programmatically, suitable for bulk assessments.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>?$select=osVersion,complianceState,lastSyncDateTime' | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response including osVersion and complianceState. Non-compliant devices require further investigation to classify patch gaps into os, driver, or uefi_bios.

option_description: Indicates whether UEFI Secure Boot is active on the device. When enabled, the firmware validates digital signatures of bootloaders and OS loaders before execution, preventing unsigned or tampered boot-time code from running.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Secure Boot Disabled Or Misconfigured' exposure (criticality: medium, score: 5) when secure_boot_enabled is false or absent. Without Secure Boot, an attacker with physical access or firmware-level write capability can implant bootkits or rootkits that persist below the OS layer and survive full OS reimaging. The policy also evaluates mdm_enrollment_status alongside this attribute, meaning managed devices are expected to enforce this control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, run the Confirm-SecureBootUEFI PowerShell cmdlet. A return value of True confirms Secure Boot is active.
how_to_obtain.command: Confirm-SecureBootUEFI
how_to_obtain.expected_output: True indicates Secure Boot is enabled. False or a cmdlet-not-supported error indicates it is disabled or unavailable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, use mokutil to query the Secure Boot state from the EFI runtime variables.
how_to_obtain.command: mokutil --sb-state
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'SecureBoot enabled' confirms the control is active. 'SecureBoot disabled' requires remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, open msinfo32 (System Information) and locate 'Secure Boot State' under System Summary. On macOS, open System Information > Software section and check 'Secure Boot'.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Windows: Start > msinfo32 > System Summary > Secure Boot State | macOS: Apple menu > About This Mac > System Report > Software > Secure Boot
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Windows: 'On'. macOS: 'Full Security' or 'Medium Security' indicates Secure Boot is functional.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM/UEM console API for the device's Secure Boot compliance attribute. In Intune, retrieve the device configuration state via Microsoft Graph.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>?$select=hardwareInformation' | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d.get('hardwareInformation',{}).get('secureBootEnabled'))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: true or false. A false value confirms the exposure condition is met.

typical_values: true (enabled — ideal for modern managed hardware)
false (disabled — legacy hardware, misconfiguration, or deliberate override)

option_description: Describes the trust state of the Secure Boot signature database (db) on the device. 'default_trusted' means only Microsoft and OEM certificates are present. 'custom_trusted' means additional enterprise or vendor certificates have been deliberately added. 'untrusted_or_unknown' means self-signed, expired, or unrecognized certificates are present in the database.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Secure Boot Disabled Or Misconfigured' when secure_boot_enabled is true but secure_boot_custom_db_state equals 'untrusted_or_unknown'. This covers the attack scenario where Secure Boot appears enabled but has been subverted by enrolling a malicious or attacker-controlled certificate into the db, allowing unsigned bootloaders signed with that certificate to execute. Custom or unknown certificates in the db effectively nullify the boot integrity guarantee.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, enumerate the Secure Boot db using PowerShell to retrieve enrolled certificate thumbprints and validate them against known Microsoft/OEM root CA values.
how_to_obtain.command: $db = Get-SecureBootUEFI -Name db; $db.bytes | ForEach-Object { [System.Security.Cryptography.X509Certificates.X509Certificate2]::new($_).Thumbprint } 2>$null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Thumbprints matching Microsoft's known Secure Boot CA values (e.g., 13adbf4309bd82709c8cd54f316ed522988a1bd4) indicate 'default_trusted'. Unknown or self-signed thumbprints indicate 'untrusted_or_unknown'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, use efi-readvar or mokutil to enumerate the db contents and inspect certificate details.
how_to_obtain.command: efi-readvar -v db 2>/dev/null || mokutil --list-enrolled 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'Subject|Issuer|Not After'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Certificates issued by Microsoft Corporation or the hardware OEM indicate 'default_trusted'. Self-signed, expired, or unrecognized issuers indicate 'untrusted_or_unknown'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the endpoint engineering team to determine whether any custom certificate enrollment scripts or MDM policies have modified the Secure Boot db, and if so, review the certificate chain of trust and expiry.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented change record showing enterprise PKI-issued, non-expired certificates were enrolled deliberately. Absence of records with unknown certs present indicates 'untrusted_or_unknown'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the UEFI firmware setup (typically F2 or Del at boot) and navigate to the Secure Boot key management section to review db entries visually.
how_to_obtain.navigation: UEFI Setup > Security > Secure Boot > Key Management > Authorized Signatures (db)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only Microsoft UEFI CA and OEM certificates listed indicates 'default_trusted'. Any unlabeled or self-signed entries indicate 'untrusted_or_unknown'.

typical_values: default_trusted (standard out-of-box configuration on managed hardware)
custom_trusted (enterprise environments with internal certificate authorities)

option_description: Reflects whether the device is actively enrolled in a Mobile Device Management (MDM) or Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) platform such as Microsoft Intune, Jamf Pro, or VMware Workspace ONE, and whether compliance policies are being enforced against it.
security_impact: The Rego policy references mdm_enrollment_status in three separate rules. It contributes to the 'Unmanaged BYOD Without MDM Enrollment' exposure when the value is 'not_enrolled' or 'enrollment_pending' combined with missing BYOD policy enforcement or remote wipe capability. It also contextually informs 'Weak Or Absent Screen Lock Authentication' and 'Secure Boot Disabled Or Misconfigured', as MDM enrollment is the primary mechanism for enforcing those controls remotely. Unenrolled devices cannot receive policy updates, compliance remediations, or remote wipe commands.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, run dsregcmd to determine the device's Azure AD and MDM join state.
how_to_obtain.command: dsregcmd /status | findstr /i 'AzureAdJoined MDMEnrolled MDMUrl'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AzureAdJoined: YES and MDMEnrolled: YES indicates 'enrolled'. MDMEnrolled: NO maps to 'not_enrolled'. Partial enrollment flows may show MDMUrl without full compliance enforcement, indicating 'enrollment_pending'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, verify MDM enrollment by checking installed configuration profiles in System Settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: macOS: System Settings > Privacy & Security > Profiles (if absent, not enrolled) | Jamf: Jamf Pro console > Computers > [Device] > Management
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more MDM-installed profiles visible indicates 'enrolled'. No profiles present indicates 'not_enrolled'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM console API to retrieve device enrollment status at scale. For Intune, use the Microsoft Graph managedDevices endpoint.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices?$filter=deviceName eq "<hostname>"&$select=deviceName,managementState,enrolledDateTime,complianceState' | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: managementState of 'managed' indicates 'enrolled'. 'retirePending' or 'unknown' maps to 'enrollment_pending'. Device absent from results indicates 'not_enrolled'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, use the profiles command-line tool to list active MDM configuration profiles.
how_to_obtain.command: profiles list -all 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'profileIdentifier|MDM|Management'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output listing MDM-related profile identifiers confirms 'enrolled'. Empty output indicates 'not_enrolled'.

typical_values: enrolled (corporate-managed devices with active MDM policy enforcement)
not_enrolled (BYOD or shadow devices, or devices that bypassed enrollment)
enrollment_pending (devices mid-onboarding or with lapsed enrollment)

option_description: Indicates whether the organization has a formally enforced BYOD policy backed by technical controls such as Azure AD Conditional Access, Okta Device Trust, or equivalent identity provider mechanisms that actively block unenrolled or non-compliant personal devices from accessing corporate applications and data.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Unmanaged BYOD Without MDM Enrollment' when mdm_enrollment_status is 'not_enrolled' or 'enrollment_pending' AND byod_policy_enforced is false. Without enforcement, unenrolled personal devices can access corporate resources with no security baseline applied — no patch requirements, no encryption verification, no EDR presence check. The absence of this control means the organization relies solely on user compliance with voluntary guidelines, which provides no technical enforcement boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Azure Active Directory, review Conditional Access policies for rules that require device compliance or hybrid join, and verify they apply to all users or the BYOD user population.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Azure Portal > Azure Active Directory > Security > Conditional Access > Policies > filter for 'Require device to be marked as compliant' or 'Require Hybrid Azure AD joined device' grant controls
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one enabled CA policy targeting corporate apps with a 'Require compliant device' grant control and no broad exclusions indicates byod_policy_enforced = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use Microsoft Graph to retrieve all Conditional Access policies and inspect their conditions and grant controls programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/identity/conditionalAccess/policies' | python3 -c "import sys,json; [print(p['displayName'], p['state'], p.get('grantControls')) for p in json.load(sys.stdin)['value']]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policies in 'enabled' state with grantControls containing 'compliantDevice' or 'domainJoinedDevice' confirm enforcement is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the IAM or security team to confirm whether a BYOD policy document exists and whether it has corresponding technical enforcement in the identity provider, not merely as a user-acknowledged agreement.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation of a Conditional Access or Device Trust policy with defined enforcement actions (block vs. allow), effective date, and user scope confirms byod_policy_enforced = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to access a corporate application (e.g., Microsoft 365, Salesforce) from an unenrolled device to verify whether access is blocked. Use a browser private mode session or a test device that is not MDM-enrolled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Access denied with an error referencing device compliance or enrollment requirement confirms byod_policy_enforced = true. Successful unrestricted access indicates byod_policy_enforced = false.

typical_values: true (organizations with mature IAM programs and zero-trust conditional access)
false (organizations relying on policy documents without technical enforcement, or small environments without enterprise IdP)

option_description: Indicates whether the IT or security team has the technical capability to remotely wipe or selectively wipe corporate data from the device via the MDM/UEM platform. Selective wipe (supported by MAM-only enrollment) removes only managed app data, while a full wipe resets the device to factory state.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Unmanaged BYOD Without MDM Enrollment' when the device is not enrolled AND remote_wipe_capability_available is false. Remote wipe is a critical incident response control for scenarios involving device loss, theft, employee termination, or confirmed compromise. Without this capability, corporate data on a lost device remains accessible indefinitely. For BYOD devices in particular, selective wipe allows corporate data removal without affecting personal data, making enrollment more acceptable to users while maintaining security.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, navigate to the specific device record and verify the availability of 'Wipe' and 'Retire' actions in the top action bar, confirming full and selective wipe capability respectively.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Intune portal > Devices > All Devices > [Device] > Overview > action buttons (Wipe, Retire, Sync)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Wipe' button present and active indicates full remote wipe capability. 'Retire' button present indicates selective/corporate data wipe is available.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Microsoft Graph API to verify available remote actions for a managed device, which includes wipe and retire actions.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>?$select=managementState,deviceActionResults,deviceName' | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A managementState of 'managed' with a valid enrolledDateTime confirms wipe actions are available. Devices in 'unknown' or absent from inventory cannot be remotely wiped.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jamf Pro (macOS/iOS), check the device's management commands section to confirm remote wipe is available. For Workspace ONE, review the device details Actions menu.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro > Computers/Devices > [Device] > Management > Management Commands | VMware Workspace ONE > Devices > [Device] > More Actions > Enterprise Wipe
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Remote Wipe' or 'Enterprise Wipe' command available in the actions menu confirms remote_wipe_capability_available = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the incident response runbook and verify whether a documented wipe procedure exists and has been tested within the past 12 months, including who holds the authorization to initiate a remote wipe.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A runbook entry with defined roles, authorization chain, and evidence of a test wipe confirms operational readiness. Absence of procedure despite technical capability may still indicate risk.

typical_values: true (MDM-enrolled devices with active Intune, Jamf, or Workspace ONE management)
false (unenrolled BYOD devices, MAM-only enrollment without wipe policy, or legacy device management)

option_description: Indicates whether a scan of the device's user-accessible file system has discovered files containing credentials, API keys, private keys, or authentication tokens in unencrypted plaintext. This includes files such as .env, config.ini, credentials.txt, id_rsa, .aws/credentials, and similar artifacts left in home directories, application data folders, or desktop locations.
security_impact: The Rego policy directly triggers 'Cleartext Credential Storage On Device' (criticality: high, score: 8) when plaintext_credential_files_found is true. This is the most direct indicator of credential exposure on the device. Plaintext credential files are high-value targets for malware, insider threats, and physical access attackers. A single compromised file can yield lateral movement credentials, cloud provider access keys, or service account tokens that extend the blast radius of a device compromise significantly beyond the device itself.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, use PowerShell to recursively scan user directories for files matching common credential file naming patterns.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-ChildItem -Path $env:USERPROFILE -Recurse -Include '*.env','credentials','*.ini','*.cfg','id_rsa','*.pem' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object FullName | ForEach-Object { Select-String -Path $_.FullName -Pattern 'password=|api_key=|secret=|token=|AWS_SECRET' -CaseSensitive:$false }
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any matching lines output indicates plaintext_credential_files_found = true. No output indicates the paths are clean.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux/macOS, use grep to search home directories and common config paths for plaintext credential patterns, and also check .aws, .ssh, and .config directories.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rEl 'password=|api_key=|AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY|PRIVATE KEY|token=' ~/.aws ~/.ssh ~/.config ~/Documents ~/Desktop 2>/dev/null | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of file paths containing matches indicates plaintext_credential_files_found = true. Empty output indicates no matches found in scanned locations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use truffleHog or git-secrets on cloned repositories or local development directories to detect secrets committed or stored in project files.
how_to_obtain.command: trufflehog filesystem --directory=$HOME/Projects --json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "import sys,json; [print(json.loads(l).get('SourceMetadata')) for l in sys.stdin if l.strip()]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output with SourceMetadata entries listing file paths confirms credential patterns were found, setting plaintext_credential_files_found = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the Windows Credential Manager and common application config directories for stored plaintext credentials using a targeted search.
how_to_obtain.command: cmdkey /list ; Get-Content "$env:APPDATA\..\Local\*\*.json" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-String -Pattern 'password|secret|token' | Select-Object -First 20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: cmdkey output lists stored credentials (though these are in the Credential Manager vault). JSON content with credential-like patterns indicates plaintext_credential_files_found = true.

typical_values: false (well-managed developer workstations with secrets management tooling, or non-developer endpoints)
true (developer workstations, DevOps-heavy environments, or endpoints where users manually handle credentials)

option_description: Indicates whether the browser's saved password store is protected by an additional authentication layer. For Firefox, this is a Primary Password (formerly Master Password). For Chromium-based browsers (Chrome, Edge), this means the OS-level credential store (Windows DPAPI tied to user session, macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service/Kwallet) is active and protecting the encrypted password database.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'Cleartext Credential Storage On Device' (criticality: high, score: 8) when browser_master_password_enforced is false. Without a master password or OS-level protection, browser-stored credentials can be decrypted by any process running in the user's session or by an attacker with physical access to the user profile directory. Browser password stores are a primary target for infostealer malware families (Redline, Vidar, Raccoon) that dump the SQLite login database and decrypt it using the accessible key. MDM policies can enforce this control on managed devices.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Firefox, check whether a Primary Password is set by examining the key4.db database — if a master password is set, a specific metadata record exists.
how_to_obtain.command: python3 -c "import sqlite3, os; db=os.path.expanduser('~/.mozilla/firefox/*.default*/key4.db'); import glob; path=glob.glob(db); conn=sqlite3.connect(path[0]) if path else None; print([r for r in conn.execute(\"SELECT item1 FROM metadata WHERE id='password'\").fetchall()] if conn else 'No Firefox profile found')"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If the query returns a non-empty item1 value, a Primary Password is set (browser_master_password_enforced = true). An empty password hash indicates no Primary Password.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, verify that Chrome/Edge uses DPAPI for password encryption by checking if the Local State file contains os_crypt configuration. The encryption key should be DPAPI-protected.
how_to_obtain.command: python3 -c "import json,os; f=open(os.path.expandvars('%LOCALAPPDATA%\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data\\Local State')); d=json.load(f); print('DPAPI protected:', d.get('os_crypt',{}).get('encrypted_key','')[:4]=='DPAPI')"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'DPAPI protected: True' confirms OS-level credential protection is active (browser_master_password_enforced = true). False indicates the key may not be properly protected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Firefox, navigate to Settings > Privacy & Security and check whether 'Use a Primary Password' checkbox is enabled. For Chrome/Edge on managed devices, check the GPO/MDM policy for PasswordManagerEnabled and related settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Firefox: Settings (about:preferences) > Privacy & Security > Logins and Passwords > Use a Primary Password | Chrome: Settings > Autofill > Password Manager | Edge: Settings > Passwords
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Firefox: 'Primary Password is set' status indicator visible. Chrome/Edge: OS-level storage confirmation or managed policy indicating credential protection is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For managed devices, query the MDM/UEM console or group policy for browser security settings. In Intune, check device configuration profiles assigned to the device for browser-related password policies.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>/deviceConfigurationStates' | python3 -c "import sys,json; [print(p['displayName'], p['state']) for p in json.load(sys.stdin).get('value',[]) if 'browser' in p['displayName'].lower() or 'password' in p['displayName'].lower()]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration profile entries for browser password policies in 'compliant' state confirm browser_master_password_enforced = true. Absence of browser security profiles indicates reliance on user configuration.

typical_values: true (Firefox with Primary Password set, or Chromium browsers on Windows with DPAPI active and user session-bound encryption)
false (default browser configuration without Primary Password, unmanaged BYOD devices, or Firefox without Primary Password enabled)

option_description: Controls whether the operating system's built-in credential manager (Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, Linux gnome-keyring/Secret Service) is actively encrypting stored credentials using session-bound keys, ensuring credentials are inaccessible when the user is not authenticated.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the cleartext_credential_storage_on_device exposure when os_credential_manager_protection_enabled is false or absent. An unprotected credential manager allows local attackers or malware running in user context to extract saved passwords, OAuth tokens, and certificates without requiring privilege escalation, directly enabling lateral movement and account takeover.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, verify DPAPI protection of Credential Manager by checking vault metadata and confirming vaultcmd lists encrypted entries.
how_to_obtain.command: vaultcmd /listcreds:"Windows Credentials" /all && reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\Protect\Providers\df9d8cd0-1501-11d1-8c7a-00c04fc297eb
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Credential entries listed with 'Protected: Yes' or DPAPI provider key present; absence of plaintext blobs in vault directory %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Vault\

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, confirm Keychain is configured to lock when the screen locks by checking security settings and login keychain lock-on-sleep status.
how_to_obtain.command: security show-keychain-info ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db 2>&1 && defaults read com.apple.screensaver askForPassword
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows 'lock-on-sleep' and 'lock-after-timeout' flags set; askForPassword returns 1

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, verify gnome-keyring is running and the default keyring is set to lock on session lock via PAM integration.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep -E 'gnome-keyring|secret-service' && grep -r 'pam_gnome_keyring' /etc/pam.d/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: gnome-keyring-daemon process visible; pam_gnome_keyring.so entries present in PAM configuration for session lock/unlock

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, open Credential Manager via Control Panel and verify stored credentials are shown as protected entries rather than plaintext.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Control Panel > User Accounts > Credential Manager > Windows Credentials — inspect each entry; protected entries show asterisks and cannot be revealed without re-authentication
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All credential entries require current user authentication to view; no plaintext passwords exposed in the GUI

typical_values: false (Linux systems without gnome-keyring PAM integration)

option_description: Indicates whether the operating system's built-in host-based firewall is active and enforcing packet filtering rules, controlling which inbound and outbound network connections are permitted on the endpoint.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers host_firewall_disabled_or_overly_permissive when host_firewall_enabled is false or not present. A disabled host firewall exposes all listening services (SMB, RDP, mDNS, application ports) to every host on the local LAN or VPN segment, enabling network-based exploitation of unpatched services without requiring any user interaction.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, query the firewall state across all network profiles (Domain, Private, Public) using netsh.
how_to_obtain.command: netsh advfirewall show allprofiles state
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each profile shows 'State ON'; any profile showing 'State OFF' indicates host_firewall_enabled = false

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, check the application-layer firewall status using socketfilterfw.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getglobalstate && sudo defaults read /Library/Preferences/com.apple.alf globalstate
how_to_obtain.expected_output: socketfilterfw returns 'Firewall is enabled' and defaults read returns 1 or 2; value 0 means disabled

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, check the status of ufw, firewalld, or raw iptables rules to determine if a host firewall is active.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo ufw status verbose 2>/dev/null || sudo firewall-cmd --state 2>/dev/null || sudo iptables -L INPUT --line-numbers -n 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ufw returns 'Status: active'; firewalld returns 'running'; iptables shows policy DROP or explicit ACCEPT rules — empty INPUT chain or ACCEPT all indicates disabled

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, verify firewall status through Windows Security Center UI.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Windows Security > Firewall & network protection — each network profile (Domain, Private, Public) should show 'Firewall is on'; a red warning icon or 'Off' status maps to host_firewall_enabled = false
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All three profiles display green status with 'on' indicator

typical_values: true (corporate-managed Windows endpoints with GPO enforcement)
false (BYOD Linux workstations without firewall configuration)
true (macOS endpoints under MDM Jamf/Intune profile)
false (developer VMs with firewall intentionally disabled)

option_description: Defines the firewall's default action for inbound network connections that do not match any explicit allow or deny rule — either blocking all unmatched traffic (deny), passing all unmatched traffic (allow_all), or in an indeterminate state (unknown).
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers host_firewall_disabled_or_overly_permissive when host_firewall_enabled is true but inbound_default_policy equals allow_all. A permissive default means even an active firewall provides no protection for services without explicit block rules, effectively negating the firewall's value and exposing listening ports to lateral movement from adjacent hosts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, retrieve the inbound firewall policy for each profile to confirm block is the default action.
how_to_obtain.command: netsh advfirewall show allprofiles firewallpolicy
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each profile shows 'Firewall Policy: BlockInbound,...'; 'AllowInbound' indicates allow_all and a misconfiguration

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, check the default policy on the INPUT chain of iptables, which governs unmatched inbound packets.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo iptables -L INPUT -n | head -3 && sudo ip6tables -L INPUT -n | head -3
how_to_obtain.expected_output: First line shows 'Chain INPUT (policy DROP)' or 'policy REJECT' for deny; 'policy ACCEPT' maps to allow_all

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, inspect the pf (packet filter) configuration for the default pass or block rule on inbound interfaces.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo pfctl -s rules 2>/dev/null | head -20 && sudo pfctl -s info 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'status\|block'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules output showing 'block in all' as implicit default; 'pass in all' or absence of block rules maps to allow_all

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux with ufw, inspect the UFW default policy configuration file to determine the configured inbound default.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '^DEFAULT_INPUT_POLICY' /etc/default/ufw
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DEFAULT_INPUT_POLICY="DROP" or "REJECT" maps to deny; "ACCEPT" maps to allow_all

typical_values: allow_all (Linux developer machines with ufw misconfigured)
deny (macOS endpoints with MDM pf profile)
unknown (endpoints with third-party firewall replacing OS firewall)

option_description: Specifies the enforcement level applied to USB mass storage devices on the endpoint — whether all USB storage is blocked outright, restricted to read-only or an approved device allowlist, or entirely unrestricted with no controls applied.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires removable_media_unrestricted directly when usb_storage_policy equals unrestricted. Unrestricted USB access enables data exfiltration of sensitive files, introduction of malware via infected drives, and BadUSB attacks where a device emulates a keyboard or network adapter. Even restricted (read-only) is insufficient for high-security environments where data ingress via USB poses supply-chain risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, check Group Policy registry keys that control removable storage device class access.
how_to_obtain.command: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\RemovableStorageDevices" /s 2>nul && reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\USBSTOR" /v Start
how_to_obtain.expected_output: USBSTOR Start value of 4 means USB storage driver disabled (blocked); Deny_All or Deny_Write keys under RemovableStorageDevices indicate restricted or blocked policy; absence or Start=3 indicates unrestricted

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, review the Device Configuration Profile assigned to the workstation for USB restriction settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Intune admin center > Devices > Configuration profiles > [Profile name] > Properties > Configuration settings > Device restrictions > General > USB connection (iOS) or Endpoint Protection > Device Control (Windows) — check 'Block removable storage' toggle
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Block removable storage set to 'Yes' = blocked; 'Read only' = restricted; 'Not configured' = unrestricted

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS with Jamf, check configuration profiles for USB storage restrictions or verify kernel extension policies blocking mass storage.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo profiles show -all 2>/dev/null | grep -A5 -i 'usb\|removable\|storage' && system_profiler SPUSBDataType 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'mass storage'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Profile output showing PayloadType com.apple.systemuiserver with mount controls, or absence of USB storage devices in system_profiler despite device being connected

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, check udev rules or udisks2 configuration for USB storage mount policies.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE '(DRIVER=="usb-storage"|udisks|SUBSYSTEM=="usb")' /etc/udev/rules.d/ && cat /etc/udisks2/udisks2.conf 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: udev rule with ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEM=="usb", RUN+="/bin/false" or similar block action = blocked; absence of rules = unrestricted

typical_values: blocked (high-security financial or government managed workstations)
restricted (standard corporate endpoints with read-only or allowlist policy)

option_description: Controls whether events related to removable media devices — including device connection, disconnection, file read, and file write operations — are captured in endpoint audit logs and forwarded to a centralized SIEM or log aggregation system.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires removable_media_unrestricted when usb_storage_policy is not blocked and removable_media_audit_enabled is false. Without audit logging, data exfiltration via USB leaves no forensic trail, preventing incident detection and making post-incident investigation impossible. Even a restricted policy requires audit evidence to demonstrate compliance and detect policy bypass attempts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, verify that audit policies for removable storage and Plug and Play events are enabled, and confirm Event ID 6416 (new external device) is being generated.
how_to_obtain.command: auditpol /get /subcategory:"Removable Storage" && auditpol /get /subcategory:"Plug and Play Events" && wevtutil qe Security /q:"*[System[EventID=6416]]" /c:5 /f:text
how_to_obtain.expected_output: auditpol shows 'Success and Failure' for Removable Storage; wevtutil returns recent Event ID 6416 entries confirming logging is active

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, verify auditd rules are configured to log USB device insertion and file access on removable mount points.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo auditctl -l | grep -E '(usb|removable|media)' && sudo grep -E '(usb|vfat|fat32)' /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Audit rules present watching /media or /run/media with -p rwa flags; auditctl -l lists active rules for removable storage paths

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Defender for Endpoint or equivalent EDR console, verify device control audit events are visible in the timeline.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft 365 Defender portal > Device inventory > [Device name] > Timeline — filter by 'Device control' event category; presence of USB connection/disconnection events confirms audit is active
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Timeline shows removable storage events with timestamps, device identifiers, and user context; no events despite USB activity indicates audit is disabled

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM, query for removable media events forwarded from the target endpoint to confirm both collection and forwarding are functioning.
how_to_obtain.command: index=endpoints sourcetype=wineventlog EventCode=6416 | stats count by host, dest_nt_host | where count > 0
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SIEM query returns rows for the target host with recent event timestamps; zero results despite known USB activity indicates removable_media_audit_enabled = false

typical_values: false (most unmanaged BYOD and small-business endpoints)
true (enterprise endpoints with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint device control)
false (Linux workstations without auditd USB rules)
true (PCI-DSS or HIPAA regulated environments with mandatory DLP logging)

option_description: Indicates whether a dedicated device control enforcement mechanism — such as an endpoint DLP agent, MDM device restriction profile, or Group Policy-based USB device class blocking — is actively installed and enforcing policy on the endpoint rather than relying solely on OS defaults.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires removable_media_unrestricted independently when device_control_tool_deployed is false, regardless of the usb_storage_policy value. Without a dedicated enforcement agent, USB policies may exist only as advisory registry keys that can be bypassed by users with local admin rights or by using alternative device classes (e.g., HID-based storage). A dedicated agent enforces policy at the kernel driver level and survives user-mode tampering.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, check for installed device control agents by querying installed software and running services associated with major DLP/device control vendors.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-WmiObject Win32_Product | Where-Object {$_.Name -match 'Symantec DLP|Digital Guardian|Ivanti|McAfee Device|Forcepoint|Trellix'} | Select Name,Version && Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.DisplayName -match 'Device Control|DLP Agent'} | Select DisplayName,Status
