how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one recognized device control product listed with running service status; no results suggests reliance on GPO-only controls or no controls

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, verify Microsoft Defender for Endpoint device control policy is active by checking the MDE sensor and device control configuration registry keys.
how_to_obtain.command: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Features" /v TamperProtection && reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Policy Manager" /v DeviceControlEnabled 2>nul
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TamperProtection value of 5 confirms MDE active; DeviceControlEnabled=1 confirms device control policy applied via Intune/MDE

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the MDM/UEM API (Intune or Jamf) to verify the device has a device control configuration profile successfully applied.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>/deviceConfigurationStates' | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A3 -i 'deviceControl\|RemovableStorage'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response shows configuration state 'compliant' for a device control or removable storage restriction profile; 'notApplicable' or absent indicates device_control_tool_deployed = false

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro, verify a device control configuration profile is scoped to and installed on the target Mac.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro > Computers > [Computer name] > Management > Configuration Profiles — look for a profile containing Privacy Preferences Policy Control or USB restrictions payloads; verify 'Last installed' date is recent
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration profile with USB/removable storage payload listed as installed; absence indicates device_control_tool_deployed = false

typical_values: true (enterprise endpoints with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint + Intune device control)
true (financial services endpoints with Symantec DLP or Digital Guardian)

option_description: Controls whether endpoint security telemetry — including authentication events, process execution records, and network connection logs — is configured to stream in near-real-time to a centralized SIEM or log aggregation platform rather than being retained only on the local device.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires endpoint_logging_and_telemetry_not_forwarded when log_forwarding_enabled is false. Logs stored only locally can be deleted or tampered with by an attacker who has compromised the device, eliminating forensic evidence of the intrusion. Centralized forwarding enables real-time detection through SIEM correlation rules, supports incident response timelines, and satisfies compliance requirements (SOC 2, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001) for log integrity.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, verify Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) subscription is active and the WinRM service is configured to forward logs to a collector.
how_to_obtain.command: wecutil es && wevtutil gl ForwardedEvents && Get-Service WinRM | Select Status && reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\EventLog\EventForwarding\SubscriptionManager"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: wecutil es lists active subscriptions; SubscriptionManager registry key contains collector server URL; WinRM service is Running

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for Sysmon, Splunk UF, Elastic Agent, or other forwarding agent processes and verify their configuration points to a live SIEM destination.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-Process -Name 'sysmon*','splunkd','elastic-agent','nxlog','winlogbeat','filebeat' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select Name,Id && netstat -ano | findstr ':9997\|:5044\|:514\|:6514'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one forwarding agent process running; netstat shows established connection to SIEM collector port (Splunk 9997, Elastic 5044, syslog 514/6514)

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, verify syslog forwarding configuration (rsyslog or syslog-ng) or Elastic/Filebeat agent is active and connected.
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl is-active rsyslog syslog-ng filebeat elastic-agent auditbeat 2>/dev/null && grep -E '^[^#].*@' /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null | head -10
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one log service active; rsyslog config shows remote forwarding directive (@@siem.corp.example.com:514); no remote target in config = log_forwarding_enabled = false

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM, confirm recent events are arriving from the target endpoint to validate active forwarding — absence of recent events despite an active device indicates forwarding is broken or disabled.
how_to_obtain.command: index=endpoints host="<workstation-hostname>" earliest=-1h | stats count by sourcetype | where count > 0
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SIEM query returns multiple sourcetypes (WinEventLog, Sysmon, etc.) with event counts > 0 within the last hour; zero results from an online device = log_forwarding_enabled = false

typical_values: true (Intune-enrolled Windows endpoints with Defender for Endpoint + MMA/AMA agent)
false (standalone Linux workstations without auditd forwarding)
true (SOC-monitored enterprise endpoints with Splunk UF or Elastic Agent deployed via MDM)

option_description: Tracks the elapsed time in hours since the SIEM or central log aggregator last received any event from this specific endpoint. A value of 9999 is assigned when the endpoint has never forwarded logs. This attribute directly reflects the health and continuity of the log forwarding pipeline from the endpoint.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the `endpoint_logging_and_telemetry_not_forwarded` exposure when `siem_last_event_age_hours > 24` even if `log_forwarding_enabled` is true, meaning a silently broken forwarder is treated as a full logging gap. Without timely SIEM ingestion, threat detection, incident response, and forensic reconstruction are all impaired. Attackers can operate undetected on endpoints that appear enrolled but are not actually reporting.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM REST API for the most recent event timestamp from the endpoint's hostname or IP address. Calculate elapsed hours from the current UTC time.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SIEM_TOKEN' 'https://<siem-host>/api/search?query=host:<hostname>&limit=1&sort=timestamp:desc' | jq '(now - (.results[0].timestamp | fromdateiso8601)) / 3600'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric value representing hours since the last event. Values under 24 are acceptable; values at or above 9999 indicate no events have ever been received.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk, run a search to find the most recent indexed event from the endpoint and compute the age in hours.
how_to_obtain.command: | makeresults | eval host="<hostname>" | appendcols [search index=endpoints host=<hostname> | head 1 | eval age_hours=round((now()-_time)/3600,1) | table age_hours]
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A decimal hour value. Zero to 1 hour is healthy; above 24 hours triggers the exposure rule.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Sentinel, navigate to Logs > query the Heartbeat table for the specific Computer name and review the TimeGenerated field of the most recent row.
how_to_obtain.command: Heartbeat | where Computer == '<hostname>' | summarize LastHeartbeat=max(TimeGenerated) | extend AgeHours=datetime_diff('hour', now(), LastHeartbeat)
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Sentinel > Logs > Run KQL query above
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AgeHours column shows elapsed time. Missing row indicates the endpoint has never sent a heartbeat (treat as 9999).

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows endpoints, check whether the log forwarding agent (e.g., Winlogbeat, NXLog, Azure Monitor Agent) service is running and review its own operational log for last successful send timestamp.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-Service -Name 'AzureMonitorAgent','winlogbeat','nxlog' | Select-Object Name,Status; Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Azure Monitor Agent/Operational' -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated,Message
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service status should be 'Running'. Event messages should show recent successful data uploads with timestamps within the last hour.

option_description: Indicates whether local endpoint logs are protected from unauthorized modification or deletion by non-privileged processes. Protection may be implemented via restrictive filesystem ACLs on log directories, EDR agent tamper-protection features, or write-once/append-only log storage configurations.
security_impact: The Rego policy includes a condition that fires `endpoint_logging_and_telemetry_not_forwarded` specifically when both `log_forwarding_enabled` is false and `log_tamper_protection_enabled` is false. Without tamper protection, an attacker who gains code execution can delete or modify local logs before they are forwarded, eliminating forensic evidence and defeating incident response timelines. This is a defense-in-depth control that preserves log integrity even when forwarding is disrupted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, check the ACLs on the Windows Event Log directory and the EDR agent installation directory to confirm non-admin users lack write or delete permissions.
how_to_obtain.command: icacls 'C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs'; icacls 'C:\Program Files\<EDR_Vendor>\' | findstr /i 'Everyone\|Users\|Authenticated'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Users and Everyone groups should have no (W), (D), or (F) permissions on the Logs directory. EDR directory should restrict modifications to SYSTEM and local Administrators only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, verify that the EDR agent tamper protection is active and that /var/log is owned by root with restrictive permissions.
how_to_obtain.command: ls -la /var/log/ | head -20; sudo /Library/Application\ Support/<EDR_Vendor>/agentctl status | grep -i tamper
how_to_obtain.expected_output: /var/log should be owned by root:wheel with permissions 755 or more restrictive. The agentctl output should confirm tamper protection is 'enabled' or 'active'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the EDR management console (e.g., CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint), navigate to the device record and verify that 'Tamper Protection' is shown as enabled in the device policy settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: EDR Console > Devices > Select Endpoint > Policy Details > Tamper Protection Status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Tamper Protection field displays 'Enabled' or 'On'. A status of 'Disabled' or absent field indicates the control is not active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the EDR management API for the tamper protection state of a specific device by its device ID.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $EDR_TOKEN' 'https://<edr-host>/api/v1/devices/<device_id>' | jq '.tamper_protection_enabled'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response should return `true`. A value of `false` or a missing field indicates tamper protection is not enforced.

option_description: Controls whether the device's Wi-Fi subsystem is configured to automatically join any open (unencrypted, no authentication required) wireless network that is within range without prompting the user for confirmation. This setting applies at the OS or MDM Wi-Fi profile level.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `automatic_wifi_association_with_untrusted_networks` when `auto_connect_to_open_networks_enabled == true` and no MDM Wi-Fi security policy is enforced. Automatic association with open networks eliminates the user as a last line of defense and exposes all unencrypted traffic to passive eavesdropping. Attackers operating rogue APs in public venues (airports, coffee shops, hotel lobbies) can silently intercept credential handshakes, session tokens, and sensitive data from devices that join automatically.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, enumerate saved Wi-Fi profiles and check whether any open-authentication profiles have connectionMode set to auto.
how_to_obtain.command: netsh wlan show profiles | ForEach-Object { if ($_ -match 'Profile\s*:\s*(.+)') { $p=$matches[1].Trim(); $details = netsh wlan show profile name=$p; if ($details -match 'Authentication\s*:\s*Open' -and $details -match 'Connection mode\s*:\s*Connect automatically') { "RISK: $p" } } }
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output indicates no open-network auto-connect profiles exist. Any line prefixed 'RISK:' identifies a profile requiring remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, inspect the Airport preferences plist for networks with Security type 'Open' and AutoJoin set to true.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo defaults read /Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/com.apple.airport.preferences | grep -A 10 'AutoJoin' | grep -B 5 '= 1'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output is the secure state. Any network entry showing AutoJoin = 1 without an associated Security key or with Security = None should be flagged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On iOS or Android managed devices, review the MDM-deployed Wi-Fi payload in the MDM console to confirm no profiles have Auto-Join enabled for open SSIDs.
how_to_obtain.navigation: MDM Console (Intune/Jamf/Workspace ONE) > Devices > Configuration Profiles > Wi-Fi Payload > Inspect each SSID entry for Auto-Join toggle and Security Type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All deployed Wi-Fi profiles should have Security Type set to WPA2/WPA3 or higher. Any profile with Security Type 'None' or 'Open' and Auto-Join enabled is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Intune Graph API to retrieve the Wi-Fi configuration profile assigned to the device and inspect the connectAutomatically and wiFiSecurityType fields.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GRAPH_TOKEN' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/deviceConfigurations?$filter=displayName eq "<profile_name>"' | jq '.value[].wifiConfigurations[] | {ssid: .ssid, connectAutomatically: .connectAutomatically, securityType: .wiFiSecurityType}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: connectAutomatically should be false for all open-type entries, or no open-type SSIDs should exist in the deployed profile.

option_description: Indicates whether the device automatically reconnects to any previously joined Wi-Fi network when an SSID matching its stored list is detected, relying solely on SSID name matching without certificate-based validation. This behavior persists in the preferred network list built up over time from user connections.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `automatic_wifi_association_with_untrusted_networks` when `auto_reconnect_to_known_networks_enabled == true` and `wifi_security_policy_enforced_via_mdm` is false. SSID-only matching is the classic precondition for evil-twin attacks: an adversary broadcasting a common SSID such as 'Starbucks', 'Airport_WiFi', or even a corporate guest network name causes the device to associate automatically. All subsequent traffic, including authentication to cloud services lacking HSTS, can be intercepted or manipulated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, list all WLAN profiles and check each for 'Connect automatically' mode, which enables SSID-based auto-reconnect.
how_to_obtain.command: netsh wlan show profiles | Select-String 'Profile' | ForEach-Object { $name = ($_ -split ':')[1].Trim(); netsh wlan show profile name=$name | Select-String 'Connection mode' }
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure profiles show 'Connection mode: Connect only if this network is broadcasting' combined with certificate trust anchors. Profiles showing 'Connect automatically' with no certificate validation are findings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, parse the Airport preferences plist to identify all networks with AutoJoin enabled, particularly those without a certificate trust anchor configured.
how_to_obtain.command: sudo /usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c 'Print :KnownNetworks' /Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/com.apple.airport.preferences.plist 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'AutoJoin|80211W|SSID_STR|SecurityType'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AutoJoin = true entries that also lack a TLSTrustExceptions or certificate configuration block should be treated as vulnerable to SSID-spoofing attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, review saved network profiles via the Settings UI and confirm that no profile is set to connect automatically without 802.1X certificate validation.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Settings > Network & Internet > Wi-Fi > Manage Known Networks > Select each network > Review 'Connect automatically when in range' checkbox and security type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The secure state is either auto-connect disabled for all non-enterprise networks, or enterprise networks enforcing certificate-based authentication (EAP-TLS).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Via Jamf Pro API, retrieve the Wi-Fi configuration profile for a device and check for AutoJoinEnabled on networks lacking certificate trust anchors.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u '$JAMF_USER:$JAMF_PASS' -H 'Accept: application/json' 'https://<jamf-host>/JSSResource/mobiledeviceconfigurations/id/<profile_id>' | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(p) for p in d.get('payloads',[]) if 'AutoJoin' in str(p)]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AutoJoin entries should only be present for profiles that also specify a PayloadCertificateAnchorUUID or equivalent trust anchor, preventing SSID-spoofing association.

option_description: Indicates whether an active MDM or UEM policy is deployed to the device that technically restricts Wi-Fi auto-join behavior and prohibits connections to open or untrusted wireless networks. This is a compensating control that can suppress the `automatic_wifi_association_with_untrusted_networks` exposure even when auto-connect settings exist at the OS level.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses `wifi_security_policy_enforced_via_mdm` as a suppression condition: both `auto_connect_to_open_networks_enabled` and `auto_reconnect_to_known_networks_enabled` only trigger the exposure when this MDM control is absent. An MDM-enforced Wi-Fi policy provides a centrally managed, tamper-resistant layer that prevents users or local malware from re-enabling unsafe connectivity behaviors that the OS permits by default. Without it, any user-level change or OS reset can re-expose the device to evil-twin attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Intune, verify that a Device Configuration Wi-Fi profile is assigned to the device's group, is in a Succeeded compliance state, and explicitly sets 'Connect automatically' to disabled for open networks.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Devices > Configuration Profiles > Filter by Platform > Select Wi-Fi profile > Monitor > Device Status > Confirm 'Succeeded' for the target device
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Device status should show 'Succeeded' for a profile that contains Wi-Fi restrictions. A status of 'Error', 'Conflict', or 'Not applicable' means the policy is not effectively enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Intune Graph API to check whether a Wi-Fi restriction configuration profile is assigned to the device and in a compliant state.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GRAPH_TOKEN' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>/deviceConfigurationStates' | jq '.value[] | select(.settingName | test("wifi|network"; "i")) | {displayName, state, settingName}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Relevant Wi-Fi setting states should show 'compliant'. Any setting showing 'notCompliant' or absent from the output indicates policy is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Jamf Pro, confirm that a Wi-Fi configuration payload with restricted Auto-Join and open-network prohibition is scoped to the device and shows a 'Managed' installation status.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro > Computers/Mobile Devices > Search for device > Management > Configuration Profiles > Verify Wi-Fi payload presence and installation status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Profile installation status should be 'Managed' or 'Installed'. Status of 'Pending', 'Failed', or absence of a Wi-Fi payload means the control is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the endpoint management team to confirm that a formally documented Wi-Fi restriction policy exists, is deployed to all applicable device groups (including BYOD enrollment profiles), and is reviewed periodically for scope completeness.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Team should be able to show the policy document, the MDM assignment groups, and evidence of last policy review. Inability to produce these artifacts indicates the policy may exist in documentation only, not in enforced deployment.

option_description: Indicates whether a technical application allowlisting or whitelisting control is actively running in enforcement mode on the endpoint, preventing execution of any binary, script, or installer not explicitly approved. Relevant technologies include Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC), AppLocker, macOS Gatekeeper with MDM enforcement, or Linux SELinux/AppArmor policies.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `shadow_it_software_and_unvetted_application_installation` when `software_allowlisting_enforced` is false, and again when a user has local_admin or full_admin rights combined with the absence of allowlisting. Without this control, users can download and execute arbitrary binaries including bundled malware, browser-delivered payloads, or supply-chain-compromised installers. Allowlisting is the highest-efficacy control for preventing execution of unapproved code and is referenced as a mitigant across multiple exposure categories in this policy set.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, check whether WDAC is deployed and in Enforced mode by inspecting the CiPolicy status via PowerShell.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard | Select-Object -ExpandProperty CodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus; Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective | Select-Object -ExpandProperty RuleCollections | Select-Object RuleCollectionType, EnforcementMode
how_to_obtain.expected_output: WDAC: CodeIntegrityPolicyEnforcementStatus should be '2' (Enforced). AppLocker: EnforcementMode should be 'Enabled' (not 'AuditOnly') for Exe, Script, Msi, and AppX rule collections.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, check the Gatekeeper enforcement state and verify it is MDM-managed (cannot be disabled by the user).
how_to_obtain.command: spctl --status; profiles -P | grep -i 'gatekeeper\|allowIdentifiedDevelopers\|EnableAssessment'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'spctl --status' should return 'assessments enabled'. The profiles output should show a configuration profile restricting Gatekeeper overrides, indicating MDM enforcement rather than user-configurable state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the MDM console (Intune, Jamf, Workspace ONE), review the Endpoint Security or Device Restrictions policy applied to the device to confirm application control is in Enforce mode, not Audit mode.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Endpoint Security > Attack Surface Reduction > Application Control Profiles > Verify policy mode is 'Enforce' not 'Audit Only'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy mode displays 'Enforce'. A mode of 'Audit Only' means the control is monitoring but not blocking unapproved software execution, which does not satisfy this attribute.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Intune Graph API to retrieve the Windows Defender Application Control policy assigned to the device and check its appLockerApplicationControl or codeIntegrityPolicies enforcement setting.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GRAPH_TOKEN' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>/deviceConfigurationStates' | jq '.value[] | select(.settingName | test("applicationControl|codeIntegrity|appLocker"; "i"))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: State should be 'compliant' with setting values indicating enforce mode. Settings showing 'notCompliant' or audit-only mode indicate the control is not fully enforced.

option_description: Indicates whether a formally documented and technically backed software vetting policy is in place that requires IT review and approval before any software can be installed on corporate or BYOD endpoints. The policy must be supported by a managed software catalog, MDM-level installation restrictions, or OS-level controls preventing self-installation without elevated approval.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `shadow_it_software_and_unvetted_application_installation` when `it_approved_software_policy_exists` is false, independent of other controls. Even when allowlisting is enforced, the absence of a documented and enforced approval policy creates governance gaps where exceptions proliferate or controls are inconsistently applied across device populations. This control addresses supply-chain risk by ensuring all installed software passes a vetting gate before deployment, reducing exposure to bundled malware, spyware-laden freeware, and compromised open-source packages.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request documentation of the IT software approval policy from the IT governance or endpoint management team. Verify that the policy specifies an approval workflow, a maintained software catalog, and defined consequences for non-compliance.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A formal policy document should exist, be version-controlled, reference an approved software catalog URL or location, and specify the approval workflow. Verbal confirmation without documentation does not satisfy this attribute.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the MDM console for device restriction policies that block user-initiated software installation and enforce installation only from an IT-managed catalog or app store.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Devices > Configuration Profiles > Device Restrictions > General > 'Block users from installing apps from unknown sources' and 'Block Google Play Store' or equivalent per-platform restriction
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Installation-blocking restrictions should be enabled. Additionally, a managed apps catalog (Company Portal, Self Service, etc.) should be deployed so users have an approved channel for software requests.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Intune Graph API to enumerate the device compliance policies and configuration restrictions applied to the device and verify that app installation restrictions are present and in a compliant state.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GRAPH_TOKEN' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/<deviceId>/deviceConfigurationStates' | jq '.value[] | select(.settingName | test("app|install|store"; "i")) | {settingName, state, setting}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Settings related to app installation should show state 'compliant' with values indicating restrictions are active. Missing entries or 'notCompliant' states indicate the policy is either absent or not enforced on this device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether a corporate app catalog (Microsoft Company Portal, Jamf Self Service, VMware Workspace ONE Catalog) is deployed and whether it is the designated channel for software requests, confirming a vetting workflow exists behind it.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jamf Pro > Self Service > Apps > Review available catalog; or Intune Admin Center > Apps > All Apps > Review approved app list and assignment status
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A populated approved software catalog should exist with documented owner and review dates per application. An empty or unmanaged catalog indicates the policy exists in name only without technical enforcement of the approval workflow.

option_description: Describes the privilege level of the primary end user's account on the device. 'standard_user' means the user cannot install software or modify system settings without admin credential elevation. 'local_admin' means the user's account is a member of the local Administrators group. 'full_admin' means the user has unrestricted control including the ability to disable security tooling. This directly governs whether security controls can be bypassed unilaterally by the user or malware running in their context.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `shadow_it_software_and_unvetted_application_installation` specifically when `endpoint_admin_rights_scope` is 'local_admin' or 'full_admin' and `software_allowlisting_enforced` is false. Admin rights amplify every other risk: malware inherits the user's token, meaning it can disable EDR agents, modify firewall rules, delete local logs (compounding the `log_tamper_protection_enabled` weakness), and install persistent backdoors. The `local_administrator_privileges_granted_to_standard_users` exposure in the Rego policy also fires when `standard_users_have_local_admin == true` without PAM enforcement, establishing this as a high-criticality standalone finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, determine whether the currently logged-in user is a member of the local Administrators group.
how_to_obtain.command: net localgroup administrators; whoami /groups | findstr /i 'S-1-5-32-544\|Administrators'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If the user's account appears in 'net localgroup administrators' output or the SID S-1-5-32-544 appears in whoami output, endpoint_admin_rights_scope is 'local_admin' or 'full_admin'. Standard users will not appear in either output.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On macOS, check whether the current user is in the admin group and whether they have unrestricted sudo access.
how_to_obtain.command: dseditgroup -o checkmember -m $(whoami) admin; sudo -l 2>/dev/null | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'dseditgroup' returns 'yes' if the user is an admin. 'sudo -l' output showing '(ALL) ALL' indicates full_admin. A standard user will see 'no' from dseditgroup and restricted or no sudo entries.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Azure AD or Active Directory via the Graph API or LDAP to retrieve the user's group memberships and identify local admin or privileged role assignments.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GRAPH_TOKEN' 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/<userPrincipalName>/memberOf?$select=displayName,groupTypes' | jq '.value[].displayName' | grep -i 'admin\|endpoint admin\|local admin'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output indicates the user holds no admin group memberships in Azure AD. Any match on admin-related group names warrants verification of whether that group grants local admin rights on the endpoint.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the MDM/UEM console, review the device record and check whether a Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) or privilege escalation management tool (CyberArk EPM, BeyondTrust, Defendpoint) is deployed and whether the user account type is reported as standard.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Devices > Select Device > Overview > Enrolled user > Check user role; or Jamf Pro > Computer > Local Accounts > Review group membership of primary user account
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Primary user account should show account type 'Standard'. Accounts listed as 'Administrator' or 'Admin' map to local_admin. Presence of a LAPS or PAM tool indicates managed elevation rather than persistent admin rights.

option_description: Controls whether a Network Access Control system (e.g., Cisco ISE, Aruba ClearPass) or an identity provider conditional access policy (e.g., Azure AD Conditional Access, Okta) is actively enforced to gate access to corporate applications, VPN, and network resources. When enabled, devices must pass an initial policy check before any resource access is permitted.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags the 'absence_of_device_compliance_check_before_resource_access' exposure when 'nac_or_conditional_access_enabled' is false or absent. Without this control, any device — including compromised, unpatched, or personally owned devices with no security controls — can freely connect to corporate resources. This is the foundational gate that makes all downstream device health checks possible; disabling it renders the entire compliance verification chain inert.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Azure AD (Entra ID), navigate to Azure Portal > Azure Active Directory > Security > Conditional Access > Policies. Confirm at least one policy exists in 'On' state targeting cloud apps or All Cloud Apps and assigned to relevant users/groups. Note any policies in 'Report-only' mode — these are NOT enforcing and must not be counted as enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Azure Portal > Azure Active Directory > Security > Conditional Access > Policies
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more policies with State = 'On' covering corporate application assignments, not merely 'Report-only'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Microsoft Graph API to enumerate conditional access policies and their enabled state. Authenticate with appropriate Graph API permissions (Policy.Read.All) and filter for policies where 'state' equals 'enabled'.
how_to_obtain.command: az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/identity/conditionalAccess/policies' --query "value[?state=='enabled'].[displayName,state,conditions.applications.includeApplications]" --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Table listing enabled policies with their display names and targeted applications; empty output or all 'disabled'/'enabledForReportingButNotEnforced' states indicates no enforcement

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Cisco ISE deployments, log into the ISE Admin console and navigate to Administration > Network Resources > Network Access Devices to confirm devices are registered, then check Policy > Policy Sets to verify active authorization policies exist. For Aruba ClearPass, navigate to Configuration > Service and confirm at least one service is enabled with enforcement profiles assigned.
how_to_obtain.navigation: ISE: Administration > Network Resources > Network Access Devices; ClearPass: Configuration > Services
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active network access devices registered and at least one enforcement policy set in 'enabled' status

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the network or identity team to determine which NAC or conditional access product is in use and request evidence of enforcement mode. Ask specifically: 'Is there any bypass or emergency access path that allows devices to connect without passing through NAC or conditional access?' Document whether any legacy VPN profiles or application endpoints are excluded from policy scope.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented confirmation that all corporate application and VPN entry points are covered by an enforced (not advisory) NAC or conditional access policy with no unguarded bypass paths

option_description: Controls whether the active NAC or conditional access policy mandates verification of specific device health signals — including OS patch level, full-disk encryption status, and EDR/antivirus agent health — as a non-negotiable condition before access is granted. This is distinct from merely having conditional access enabled; the policy must be configured to evaluate and enforce device compliance state, not just user identity.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'absence_of_device_compliance_check_before_resource_access' exposure when 'nac_or_conditional_access_enabled' is true but 'device_health_checks_enforced' is false. This scenario is particularly dangerous because it creates a false sense of security — the organization believes access is controlled, but unpatched, unencrypted, or EDR-absent devices pass through unchecked. The control must validate patch currency, encryption status, and endpoint protection agent health to close the compliance verification gap exploited by this rule.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Azure AD Conditional Access, open each enabled policy and inspect the 'Grant' conditions. Confirm 'Require device to be marked as compliant' or 'Require Hybrid Azure AD joined device' is selected. Then navigate to Endpoint Manager (Intune) > Devices > Compliance Policies to verify compliance policies are created that check encryption status (BitLocker), OS patch level (minimum OS version), and EDR health (Microsoft Defender health or third-party connector). Confirm policies are assigned to device groups.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Azure Portal > Azure AD > Security > Conditional Access > [Policy] > Grant; Microsoft Intune > Devices > Compliance Policies
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Require device to be marked as compliant' is checked in Grant controls, and corresponding compliance policies evaluate patch level, encryption, and EDR health

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Microsoft Graph to retrieve conditional access grant controls and Intune compliance policy settings to verify health signals are required, not advisory.
how_to_obtain.command: az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/identity/conditionalAccess/policies' --query "value[?state=='enabled'].{Name:displayName, GrantControls:grantControls.builtInControls}" --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Grant controls include 'compliantDevice' or 'domainJoinedDevice' for enforced policies; absence of these values means health checks are not a grant condition

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Okta deployments, use the Okta API to inspect device assurance policies which define health signal requirements. Confirm policies check platform patch version, disk encryption, and security software presence, and that these policies are bound to application sign-on rules.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: SSWS <api_token>' -H 'Accept: application/json' 'https://<okta_domain>/api/v1/device-assurances' | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response listing device assurance policies with diskEncryptionType, osVersion constraints, and secureHardwarePresent conditions defined; policies must be referenced in app sign-on rules to be enforced

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the compliance policy configuration documentation from the endpoint management team. Specifically ask for evidence that non-compliant devices (e.g., those missing EDR, unencrypted, or behind on patches) are actually blocked or quarantined rather than receiving a warning and proceeding. Request a compliance report showing what percentage of devices are currently flagged non-compliant and what their access status is.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation confirming specific health signal checks (patch level, encryption, EDR) are required conditions in compliance policy, with evidence that non-compliant devices do not receive unrestricted access

option_description: Defines the enforcement action applied by the NAC or conditional access policy when a device fails device health posture checks. The four possible actions are: 'block' (access is denied entirely), 'quarantine' (device is isolated to a restricted network segment, typically for remediation), 'allow_with_warning' (access is permitted but the user receives a notification), and 'allow_unrestricted' (access is fully granted despite compliance failure, effectively bypassing enforcement).
security_impact: The Rego policy explicitly triggers the 'absence_of_device_compliance_check_before_resource_access' exposure when 'non_compliant_device_action' is set to 'allow_with_warning' or 'allow_unrestricted', even if 'nac_or_conditional_access_enabled' and 'device_health_checks_enforced' are both true. This is a critical subtlety: an organization can have both prior controls correctly enabled but completely negate their value by choosing a permissive action for non-compliant devices. Only 'block' or 'quarantine' constitutes genuine enforcement; the other two values mean compromised, unencrypted, or EDR-absent devices can freely access corporate resources, satisfying the letter but not the intent of compliance policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Azure AD Conditional Access, open each enforced policy and review the 'Grant' section. If 'Require device to be marked as compliant' is set, the platform action for non-compliant devices is 'block' by default. However, also check for any named locations, terms-of-use bypass, or session controls that might allow access with reduced controls. In Microsoft Intune, navigate to Devices > Compliance Policies > [Policy] > Actions for noncompliance to review whether the action is 'Mark device noncompliant' (block access via conditional access) or merely 'Send email to end user' (allow with warning only).
how_to_obtain.navigation: Intune Admin Center > Devices > Compliance Policies > [Policy] > Actions for noncompliance
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Actions for noncompliance should show 'Mark device noncompliant' with a grace period of 0 days (immediate) or a very short window; actions limited to 'Send email' without noncompliant marking indicate allow_with_warning behavior

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve Intune compliance policy scheduled actions via Microsoft Graph to confirm the noncompliance action and grace period configured for each policy.
how_to_obtain.command: az rest --method GET --url 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/deviceCompliancePolicies' --query "value[].{Name:displayName, ScheduledActions:scheduledActionsForRule[].scheduledActionConfigurations[].{Action:actionType,GracePeriodHours:gracePeriodHours}}" --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each compliance policy should show 'block' as actionType with gracePeriodHours of 0 or a minimal value; 'notification' without a corresponding 'block' action maps to allow_with_warning

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Cisco ISE, navigate to Policy > Policy Sets > [Relevant Policy Set] > Authorization Policy and inspect the authorization profile assigned to devices that fail posture assessment. The profile should assign a 'Quarantine' VLAN or ACL (e.g., dACL DENY_ALL or redirect to remediation portal) rather than a 'PermitAccess' profile. For Aruba ClearPass, review Configuration > Enforcement > Enforcement Profiles assigned to the 'Unhealthy' posture condition and confirm it enforces VLAN quarantine or blocks access.
how_to_obtain.navigation: ISE: Policy > Policy Sets > Authorization Policy (posture noncompliant condition); ClearPass: Configuration > Enforcement > Enforcement Profiles
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-compliant posture condition maps to a Quarantine VLAN, dACL DENY_ALL, or captive portal redirect — not a PermitAccess profile or no-enforcement profile

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review NAC or conditional access sign-in logs to observe what actually happens to non-compliant devices in practice. In Azure AD, use the Sign-in logs filtered by 'Device compliant = No' to see the resulting access outcome. Devices that successfully sign in despite non-compliant status indicate the enforcement action is 'allow_with_warning' or 'allow_unrestricted' in practice.
how_to_obtain.command: az rest --method GET --url "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/auditLogs/signIns?\$filter=deviceDetail/isCompliant eq false&\$top=50" --query "value[].{User:userPrincipalName, App:appDisplayName, Compliant:deviceDetail.isCompliant, Result:status.errorCode}" --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Sign-ins from non-compliant devices should show errorCode 53003 (blocked by conditional access) or equivalent block/quarantine indicator; errorCode 0 (success) for non-compliant devices confirms the enforcement action is permissive
